Which of the following statements is/are true?

  1. $\text{LL(1)}$ parser uses backtracking
  2. For a grammar to be $\text{LL(1)}$, it must be left-recursive
  3. For a grammar to be $\text{LL(1)}$, it must be left-factored
  4. The $\text{LL(1)}$ parsers are more powerful than the SLR parsers

options.label: C

questions.explanation: $\boxed{\text{Answer: C}}$ Watch detailed discussion on this question $\text{LL(1)}$ parser uses backtracking. $\ \textcolor{red}{\boxed{\text{False}}}$ No, $\text{LL(1)}$ parser is a predictive parser. When expanding a nonterminal, $\text{LL(1)}$ parser predict the production to use by looking at the next token of the input. The decision is forced.  So, $\text{LL(1)}$ parser is not using backtracking. For a grammar to be $\text{LL(1)}$, it must be left-recursive. $\ \textcolor{red}{\boxed{\text{False}}}$ No. In fact for a grammar to be $\text{LL(1)}$, it must not be left-recursive. Since left-recursive grammar can never be $\text{LL(1)}$. Proof1   Proof2 For a grammar to be $\text{LL(1)}$, it must be left-factored. $\ \textcolor{blue}{\boxed{\text{True}}}$ Yes, because non-left-factored grammar can never be $\text{LL(1)}$. questions.excerpt: Consider the following two syntax-directed definitions $\text{SDD1}$ and $\text{SDD2}$ for type declarations.\[\renewcommand{\arraystretch}{1.3}\begin{array}{|l|l|}\hline...
questions.questionText: Consider the following two syntax-directed definitions $\text{SDD1}$ and $\text{SDD2}$ for type declarations. \[ \renewcommand{\arraystretch}{1.3} \begin{array}{|l|l|} \hline {\textbf{SDD1}} \\ \hline { \begin{array}{c} \textbf{Grammar} \\ (G_1) \end{array}} & {\textbf{Semantic Rules}} \\ \hline \hline D \rightarrow TV & \begin{array}{l} D.type = T.type \\ V.type = T.type \end{array} \\ \hline T \rightarrow \text{int} & T.type = \text{int} \\ \hline T \rightarrow \text{float} & T.type = \text{float} \\ \hline V \rightarrow V_1\ \text{id} & \begin{array}{l} V_1.type = V.type \\ \text{put(id.entry, V.type)} \end{array} \\ \hline V \rightarrow \text{id} & \text{put(id.entry, V.type)} \\ \hline \end{array} \] \[ \renewcommand{\arraystretch}{1.3} \begin{array}{|l|l|} \hline {\textbf{SDD2}} \\ \hline { \begin{array}{c} \textbf{Grammar} \\ (G_2) \end{array}} & {\textbf{Semantic Rules}} \\ \hline \hline D \rightarrow D_1\ \text{id} & \begin{array}{l} D.type = D_1.type \\ \text{put(id.entry, D_1.type)} \end{array} \\ \hline D \rightarrow T\ \text{id} & \begin{array}{l} D.type = T.type \\ \text{put(id.entry, T.type)} \end{array} \\ \hline T \rightarrow \text{int} & T.type = \text{int} \\ \hline T \rightarrow \text{float} & T.type = \text{float} \\ \hline \end{array} \] $D$ is the start symbol, and int, float and id are the three terminals. The non-terminal $V_{1}$ is the same as $V$ and the non-terminal $D_{1}$ is the same as $D$. Here, the subscript is used to differentiate the grammar symbols on the two sides of a production. The function put updates the symbol table with the type information for an identifier. Let $\text{P}$ and $\text{Q}$ be the languages specified by grammars $\text{G1}$ and $\text{G2}$, respectively. Which of the following statements is/are true? The languages $\text{P}$ and $\text{Q}$ are the same $\text{SDD2}$ is $\text{S}$-attributed and contains only synthesized attributes $\text{SDD1}$ is $\text{L}$-attributed and contains only inherited attributes The specifications of $\text{SDD1}$ and $\text{SDD2}$ are such that the same entries get added to the symbol table

SDD1 $$ \begin{array}{|c|c|} \hline \textbf{Grammar} & \textbf{Semantic\ Rule} \\ \hline D \rightarrow TV & D.type = T.type \\ & V.type = T.type \\ \hline T \rightarrow int & T.type = int \\ \hline T \rightarrow float & T.type = float \\ \hline V \rightarrow V_1\, id & V.type = V_1.type \\ & Put(id.entry,\;V_1.type) \\ \hline V \rightarrow id & Put(id.entry,\;V.type) \\ \hline \end{array} $$ SDD2 $$ \begin{array}{|c|c|} \hline \textbf{Grammar} & \textbf{Semantic\ Rule} \\ \hline D \rightarrow D_1\, id & D.type = D_1.type \\ & Put(id.entry,\;D_1.type) \\ \hline D \rightarrow T\, id & D.type = T.type \\ & Put(id.entry,\;T.type) \\ \hline T \rightarrow int & T.type = int \\ \hline T \rightarrow float & T.type = float \\ \hline \end{array} $$ Which of the following is/are correct?  SDD2 is S-attributed and contains only synthesized attributes. questions.questionText: A lexical analyzer is designed for a new language with the following rules for token generation: $\mathrm{KEYWORD1}: \verb|if|$ $\mathrm{KEYWORD2}: \verb|iff|$ $\mathrm{IDENTIFIER}: \verb|[a-z]+|$ (One or more lowercase letters) $\mathrm{OPERATOR}: \verb|+| , \verb|++|$ The scanner follows the Longest Match Rule (Maximal Munch) and breaks ties using Rule Priority (the order listed above). Consider the input string$: \verb|ifffff++|$ Which of the following statement(s) is/are TRUE regarding the tokens generated? THE SCANNER GENERATES A TOTAL OF $3$ TOKENS.  THE FIRST TOKEN GENERATED IS $\verb|iff| ~\mathrm{(KEYWORD2)}$.  THE STRING IS PRE-PROCESSED INTO $\verb|iff|$, $\verb|ffff|$, AND $\verb|++|$.  IF THE INPUT WAS $\verb|if+|$, THE SCANNER WOULD GENERATE $\verb|if| ~\mathrm{(KEYWORD1)}$ AND $\verb|+| ~\mathrm{(OPERATOR)}$.
questions.questionHtml:
A lexical analyzer is designed for a new language with the following rules for token generation:

  1. $\mathrm{KEYWORD1}: \verb|if|$
     
  2. $\mathrm{KEYWORD2}: \verb|iff|$
     
  3. $\mathrm{IDENTIFIER}: \verb|[a-z]+|$ (One or more lowercase letters)
     
  4. $\mathrm{OPERATOR}: \verb|+| , \verb|++|$

The scanner follows the Longest Match Rule (Maximal Munch) and breaks ties using Rule Priority (the order listed above).

Consider the input string$: \verb|ifffff++|$

Which of the following statement(s) is/are TRUE regarding the tokens generated?

  1. THE SCANNER GENERATES A TOTAL OF $3$ TOKENS. 
     
  2. THE FIRST TOKEN GENERATED IS $\verb|iff| ~\mathrm{(KEYWORD2)}$. 
     
  3. THE STRING IS PRE-PROCESSED INTO $\verb|iff|$, $\verb|ffff|$, AND $\verb|++|$. 
     
  4. IF THE INPUT WAS $\verb|if+|$, THE SCANNER WOULD GENERATE $\verb|if| ~\mathrm{(KEYWORD1)}$ AND $\verb|+| ~\mathrm{(OPERATOR)}$.

options.label: A
options.text: THE SCANNER GENERATES A TOTAL OF $3$ TOKENS.

options.label: C
options.text: THE STRING IS PRE-PROCESSED INTO $\verb|iff|$, $\verb|ffff|$, AND $\verb|++|$.

options.label: D
options.text: IF THE INPUT WAS $\verb|if+|$, THE SCANNER WOULD GENERATE $\verb|if| ~\mathrm{(KEYWORD1)}$ AND $\verb|+| ~\mathrm{(OPERATOR)}$.

questions.explanation: Correct answer is D. From the start ( i ): if → length 2 iff → length 3 [a–z]+ → matches the whole letter run ifffff → length 6 Longest is length 6 ⇒ IDENTIFIER("ifffff") Remaining: ++ ++ vs + ⇒ longest is ++ ⇒ OPERATOR("++") So tokens are: IDENTIFIER ifffff OPERATOR ++ Total = 2 tokens . A. 3 tokens → False (there are 2). B. First token is iff → False (it’s an identifier ifffff ). C. Pre-processed into iff , ffff , ++ → False (lexer doesn’t pre-split; maximal munch gives ifffff ). D. For input if+ : if matches KEYWORD1 and IDENTIFIER with same length (2). Tie → rule priority ⇒ KEYWORD1. Then + ⇒ OPERATOR. Hence, D is true.

If a lexical analyzer is implemented using a Non-deterministic Finite Automaton (NFA), it will always be more space-efficient than a DFA implementation, but might be slower in terms of time complexity.  The language $L=\left\{a^n b^n \mid n \geq 0\right\}$ cannot be recognized by a lexical analyzer.
questions.questionHtml:
Which of the following statement(s) is/are TRUE regarding Lexical Analysis and Regular Expressions?

  1. The number of states in a minimal Deterministic Finite Automaton (DFA) for the language $L=\left\{w \in\{a, b\}^* \mid\right.~w \text{contains 'aba' as a substring\}}$ is $4$.
     
  2. If a lexical analyzer is implemented using a Non-deterministic Finite Automaton (NFA), it will always be more space-efficient than a DFA implementation, but might be slower in terms of time complexity. 
     
  3. The language $L=\left\{a^n b^n \mid n \geq 0\right\}$ cannot be recognized by a lexical analyzer.

options.label: A
options.text: The number of states in a minimal Deterministic Finite Automaton (DFA) for the language $L=\left\{w \in\{a, b\}^* \mid\right.~w \text{contains 'aba' as a substring\}}$ is $4$.

options.label: B
options.text: If a lexical analyzer is implemented using a Non-deterministic Finite Automaton (NFA), it will always be more space-efficient than a DFA implementation, but might be slower in terms of time complexity.

options.label: C
options.text: The language $L=\left\{a^n b^n \mid n \geq 0\right\}$ cannot be recognized by a lexical analyzer.

questions.explanation: Statement I (TRUE): To recognize a substring of length $n$ (like "aba", where $n=3$ ), a minimal DFA generally requires $n+1$ states. For "$aba$", the states represent$: (1)$ Initial/nothing, $(2)$ '$a$' seen, $(3) $'$ab$' seen, and $(4)$ '$aba$' seen (final state). Statement II (FALSE): While an NFA can be more space-efficient (fewer states) than a DFA, it is not "always" the case for every implementation. Furthermore, lexical analyzers in practice (like Flex) almost always convert the NFA to a DFA to ensure $O(1)$ time complexity per character, prioritizing speed over theoretical space savings. Statement III (TRUE): The language $L=\left\{a^n b^n \mid n \geq 0\right\}$ is a Context-Free Language that is not regular. Since lexical analyzers are based on Finite Automata (which have no memory/count mechanism), they cannot recognize languages that require matching or counting, such as $a^n b^n$. \end{gathered}

questions.explanation: Detailed Video Explanation with Easy Proof (Click Here) In a semantic rule, if an inherited attribute of a nonterminal $B$ is defined, then $B$ must be on the RHS of the corresponding production. Hence, that semantic rule is associated with the production at the parent of $B$. An inherited attribute for a nonterminal $B$ at a parse-tree node $N$ is defined by a semantic rule associated with the production at the parent of $N$. Note that the production must have $B$ as a symbol in its body. An inherited attribute at node $N$ is defined only in terms of attribute values at $N$'s parent, $N$ itself, and $N$'s siblings. A synthesized attribute for a nonterminal $A$ at a parse-tree node $N$ is defined by a semantic rule associated with the production at $N$. Note that the production must have $A$ as its head. A synthesized attribute at node $N$ is defined only in terms of attribute values at the children of $N$ and at $N$ itself. GO Classes answered Feb 1 • edited Feb 1 by Deepak Poon

Consider the following L-attributed Syntax Directed Definition (SDD). $S$ is the start symbol, and S.val is a synthesized attribute. A.inh is an inherited attribute.

  2. $A \rightarrow id \quad\{ A.val = A.inh × id.lexval \}$
     
  3. $B \rightarrow id \quad\{B. val = id.lexval +2\}$
     

For the input string id id where the lexical values of the two id tokens are $\mathbf{3}$ and $\mathbf{4}$ respectively, what is the value of $S.val$?

  1. $15$
     
  2. $21$
     
  3. $23$
     
  4. $25$
questions.explanation: This problem involves an L-attributed definition , where inherited attributes $($like $A.inh)$ are passed down or across the tree, and synthesized attributes (like $S.val$ and $A.val)$ are passed up. Initialize $A.inh:$ According to the first production, $A.inh$ is set to $5$. Evaluate $A.val:$ The second production states $A.val =A . i n h \times \mathrm{id}_1. lexval$ . Given $\mathrm{id}_1.lexval =3$ : $A.val =5 \times 3=15$. Evaluate  $B.val:$ The third production states $B.val =\mathrm{id}_2.lexval +2$. Given $\mathrm{id}_2.lexval =4$ : $B.val =4+2=6$. Evaluate  $S.val:$ Finally, $S.val = A.val + B.val$. $S.val =15+6=21$. questions.explanation: Since $\mathrm{follow(r)}$ contains '$=$' Hence option C is correct. That's why $\mathrm{A}, \mathrm{B}$ are incorrect. why it is $l r(1)$ ? an $\operatorname{lr}(1)$ parser uses specific lookaheads rather than the global follow set. when we build $\operatorname{lr}(1)$ items for state $i_2$, the lookaheads are restricted: $[s \rightarrow l \cdot=r, \mathbb{\$}]$ $[r \rightarrow l, \mathrm{~S}]$ the resolution: the shift action $(s \rightarrow l \cdot=r)$ only happens if the next symbol is $=$. the reduction  $(r \rightarrow l \cdot)$ only happens if the next symbol is $\$$. since $=$ and $\$$ are distinct, there is no conflict in $\operatorname{lr}(1)$. in this grammar, merging states does not create any new conflicts that weren't already there in the $\operatorname{lr}(1)$ table. questions.questionHtml:
Consider the following basic block of three-address code:

  1. $\mathrm{t 1=a+b}$
     
  2. $\mathrm{t 2=c* d}$
     
  3. $\mathrm{t} 3=\mathrm{t} 1+\mathrm{t} 2$
     
  4. $\mathrm{a=t 3}$
     
  5. $\mathrm{t 4=c*d}$
     
  6. $\mathrm{b}=\mathrm{t} 1+\mathrm{t} 4$

Assuming '$\mathrm{a}$' and '$\mathrm{b}$' are live at the end of the block, which of the following represents the optimized code after applying Common Subexpression Elimination (CSE) and Copy Propagation?

  1. $\mathrm{t 1=a+b ; ~t 2=c* d ; ~a=t 1+t 2 ; ~b=t 1+t 2}$
     
  2. $\mathrm{t1 = a + b; ~t2 = c * d; ~t3 = t1 + t2; ~a = t3; ~t4 = c * d; b = t1 + t4}$
     
  3. $\mathrm{t 1=a+b ; ~t 2=c* d ; ~a=t 1+t 2 ; ~b=a}$
     
  4. $\mathrm{t1= a+b; ~a = t1+ (c*d); ~b = t1 + (c*d)}$

options.label: B
options.text: $\mathrm{t1 = a + b; ~t2 = c * d; ~t3 = t1 + t2; ~a = t3; ~t4 = c * d; b = t1 + t4}$

questions.explanation: Common Subexpression Elimination (CSE) In line $5, ~\mathrm{c * d}$ is a common subexpression already computed in line $2$ and stored in $\mathrm{t 2}. We replace $\mathrm{t 4=c * d}$ with $\mathrm{t 4=t 2}$. Now line $6$ becomes $\mathrm{b=t 1+t 2}$.  Notice that $+1++2$ was already computed in line $3$ and stored in $+3$. Thus, we can replace the expression in line $6$ with $\mathrm{t 3}$, making it $\mathrm{b}=\mathrm{t} 3$. Copy Propagation In line $4$, $\mathrm{a=t 3}$. Since $\mathrm{a}$ is now a copy of $\mathrm{t 3}$, we can propagate this. In line $6$, instead of $\mathrm{b=t 3}$, we can use the value assigned to $\mathrm{a}$. The final optimized assignments for the live variables $\mathrm{a}$ and $\mathrm{b}$ both rely on the shared computation of $\mathrm{t1 + t2}$. Final optimized code: $$ \begin{aligned} & t 1=a+b \\ & t 2=c * d \\ & a=t 1+t 2 \\ & b=a \end{aligned} $$ GO Classes answered Jan 29 GO Classes comment Share Follow 0 reply Please log in or

questions.questionText: Consider the following regular expression over the alphabet $\{a, b\}$ used for a lexical analyzer token definition: $$ R=(a+b)^*(a a+b b)(a+b)^* $$ Which of the following describes the language $L(R)$ and the properties of its corresponding Minimal Deterministic Finite Automata (MDFA)? THE LANGUAGE CONSISTS OF ALL STRINGS CONTAINING AT LEAST ONE PAIR OF CONSECUTIVE IDENTICAL SYMBOLS, AND THE MDFA HAS $3$ STATES. THE LANGUAGE CONSISTS OF ALL STRINGS ENDING WITH $aa$ OR $bb$, AND THE MDFA HAS $4$ STATES. THE LANGUAGE CONSISTS OF ALL STRINGS CONTAINING AT LEAST ONE PAIR OF CONSECUTIVE IDENTICAL SYMBOLS, AND THE MDFA HAS $4$ STATES. THE LANGUAGE CONSISTS OF ALL STRINGS WHERE EVERY $a$ IS FOLLOWED BY ANOTHER $a$, AND THE MDFA HAS $2$ STATES.

R=(a+b)^*(a a+b b)(a+b)^*
$$

questions.questionText: Consider the following SDT scheme used to evaluate an expression. The synthesized attribute $\mathrm{val}$ stores the numerical value. \[ \begin{aligned} E &\rightarrow E_1 + T \quad \{\, E.\text{val} = E_1.\text{val} + T.\text{val} \,\} \\ E &\rightarrow T \quad \{\, E.\text{val} = T.\text{val} \,\} \\ T &\rightarrow T_1 * F \quad \{\, T.\text{val} = T_1.\text{val} \times F.\text{val} \,\} \\ T &\rightarrow F \quad \{\, T.\text{val} = F.\text{val} \,\} \\ F &\rightarrow (E) \quad \{\, F.\text{val} = E.\text{val} \,\} \\ F &\rightarrow \text{digit} \quad \{\, F.\text{val} = \text{digit.lexval} \,\} \end{aligned} \] For the input string $3 * 4+5 *(2+1)$, what is the value of $E.\mathrm{val}$ at the root of the dependency graph?
questions.questionHtml:
Consider the following SDT scheme used to evaluate an expression. The synthesized attribute $\mathrm{val}$ stores the numerical value.
\[
\begin{aligned}
E &\rightarrow E_1 + T \quad \{\, E.\text{val} = E_1.\text{val} + T.\text{val} \,\} \\
E &\rightarrow T \quad \{\, E.\text{val} = T.\text{val} \,\} \\
T &\rightarrow T_1 * F \quad \{\, T.\text{val} = T_1.\text{val} \times F.\text{val} \,\} \\
T &\rightarrow F \quad \{\, T.\text{val} = F.\text{val} \,\} \\
F &\rightarrow (E) \quad \{\, F.\text{val} = E.\text{val} \,\} \\
F &\rightarrow \text{digit} \quad \{\, F.\text{val} = \text{digit.lexval} \,\}
\end{aligned}
\]
For the input string $3 * 4+5 *(2+1)$, what is the value of $E.\mathrm{val}$ at the root of the dependency graph?
questions.explanation: $E.\mathrm{val}=12+15=27.$ GO Classes answered Jan 29 GO Classes comment Share Follow 0 reply Please log in or register to add a comment. questions.questionText: Consider the following grammar $G$ with terminal set $\Sigma=\{a, b, c, d\}$ and non-terminal set $V=\{S, A, B\}$ : $$ \begin{gathered} S \rightarrow a A b \mid b B a \\ A \rightarrow c S \mid \epsilon \\ B \rightarrow d S \mid \epsilon \end{gathered} $$ Which of the following statements is/are CORRECT regarding the $\mathrm{LL(1)}$ parsing table for grammar $G$ ? THE $\mathrm{FIRST}(S)$ SET CONTAINS $\{a, b\}$. THE $\mathrm{FOLLOW}(A)$ SET CONTAINS $\{b\}$. THERE IS A REDUCE-REDUCE CONFLICT IN THE PARSING TABLE. THE GRAMMAR $G$ IS $\mathrm{LL(1)}$.
questions.questionHtml:
Consider the following grammar $G$ with terminal set $\Sigma=\{a, b, c, d\}$ and non-terminal set $V=\{S, A, B\}$ :

$$
\begin{gathered}
S \rightarrow a A b \mid b B a \\
A \rightarrow c S \mid \epsilon \\
B \rightarrow d S \mid \epsilon
\end{gathered}
$$


Which of the following statements is/are CORRECT regarding the $\mathrm{LL(1)}$ parsing table for grammar $G$ ?

  1. THE $\mathrm{FIRST}(S)$ SET CONTAINS $\{a, b\}$.
     
  2. THE $\mathrm{FOLLOW}(A)$ SET CONTAINS $\{b\}$.
     
  3. THERE IS A REDUCE-REDUCE CONFLICT IN THE PARSING TABLE.
     
  4. THE GRAMMAR $G$ IS $\mathrm{LL(1)}$.

options.label: C
options.text: THERE IS A REDUCE-REDUCE CONFLICT IN THE PARSING TABLE.

questions.explanation: FIRST Sets $\operatorname{FIRST}(S)=\{a, b\}$ $\operatorname{FIRST}(A)=\{c, \epsilon\}$ $\operatorname{FIRST}(B)=\{d, \epsilon\}$ FOLLOW Sets $\operatorname{FOLLOW}(S)=\{\$\} \cup\{\operatorname{FIRST}(b)$ from $S \rightarrow a A b\} \cup\{F I R S T(a)$ from $S \rightarrow b B a\}$ $\operatorname{FOLLOW}(S)=\{\$, b, a\}$ $\operatorname{FOLLOW}(A)=\{b\}($ from $S \rightarrow a A b)$ $\operatorname{FOLLOW}(B)=\{a\}($ from $S \rightarrow b B a)$ (A) IS CORRECT: $F I R S T(S)=\{a, b\}$. (B) IS CORRECT: FOLLOW $(A)=\{b\}$. (C) IS INCORRECT: There are no conflicts; it is a deterministic $L L(1)$ table. (D) IS CORRECT: The grammar satisfies all $L L(1)$ conditions.

questions.questionText: Consider the following sequence of three-address code (TAC) instructions: 1. i = 1 2. j = 1 3. t1 = 5 * i 4. t2 = t1 + j 5. a[t2] = 0 6. j = j + 1 7. if j <= 5 goto (3) 8. i = i + 1 9. if i <= 5 goto (2) Which of the following optimization techniques can be successfully applied to this code to reduce the number of multiplications performed inside the inner loop? CONSTANT FOLDING CODE MOTION LOOP UNROLLING DEAD CODE ELIMINATION
questions.questionHtml:
Consider the following sequence of three-address code (TAC) instructions:

1. i = 1
2. j = 1
3. t1 = 5 * i
4. t2 = t1 + j
5. a[t2] = 0
6. j = j + 1
7. if j <= 5 goto (3)
8. i = i + 1
9. if i <= 5 goto (2)

Which of the following optimization techniques can be successfully applied to this code to reduce the number of multiplications performed inside the inner loop?

  1. CONSTANT FOLDING
     
  2. CODE MOTION
     
  3. LOOP UNROLLING
     
  4. DEAD CODE ELIMINATION
questions.explanation: Analysis: In the inner loop $($instructions $3-7)$, the expression $\verb|t1 = 5 * i|$ is calculated. However, $\verb|i|$ is constant relative to the inner loop; it only changes in the outer loop $($instruction $8)$. Code Motion: Specifically, $\verb|t1 = 5 * i|$ is a loop-invariant for the inner loop and can be moved outside to the outer loop. This reduces the total number of multiplications from $25$ down to $5$. GO Classes answered Jan 27 GO Classes comment Share Follow 0 reply Please log in or register to add a comment. Consider the following grammar $G$ with start symbol $S$ :

$$
\begin{aligned}

& S \rightarrow R \\
& L \rightarrow * R \\
& L \rightarrow i d . \\
& R \rightarrow L
\end{aligned}
$$


Let $I$ be the set of $L R(1)$ items. During the construction of the canonical $L R(1)$ parsing table, a state contains the following items:

$$
\begin{aligned}
& L \rightarrow i d \cdot,[=] \\
& R \rightarrow L^{\cdot},[\$]
\end{aligned}
$$


Which of the following statements is TRUE regarding this state?

  1. THERE IS A SHIFT-REDUCE CONFLICT.
     
  2. THERE IS A REDUCE-REDUCE CONFLICT.
     
  3. THERE IS NO CONFLICT IN THIS STATE FOR AN $\mathrm{LR(1)}$ PARSER.
     
  4. THIS STATE WILL RESULT IN A REDUCE-REDUCE CONFLICT ONLY IN AN $\mathrm{SLR(1)}$ PARSER.

options.label: C
options.text: THERE IS NO CONFLICT IN THIS STATE FOR AN $\mathrm{LR(1)}$ PARSER.

options.label: D
options.text: THIS STATE WILL RESULT IN A REDUCE-REDUCE CONFLICT ONLY IN AN $\mathrm{SLR(1)}$ PARSER.

questions.questionText: Consider the following basic block of Three-Address Code: 1. a = 1 2. b = a + 1 3. c = a + b 4. a = c + b 5. return a A variable is live at a point if its current value will be used in the future before being redefined. Assuming only the variable $\mathrm{a}$ is live at the exit of this block, which variables are live immediately after statement $2$ has executed? $\{\mathrm{a, b}\}$ $\{\mathrm{b, c}\}$ $\{\mathrm{a}, \mathrm{b}, \mathrm{c}\}$ $\{\mathrm{a, c}\}$
questions.questionHtml:
Consider the following basic block of Three-Address Code:

1. a = 1
2. b = a + 1
3. c = a + b
4. a = c + b
5. return a

A variable is live at a point if its current value will be used in the future before being redefined. Assuming only the variable $\mathrm{a}$ is live at the exit of this block, which variables are live immediately after statement $2$ has executed?

  1. $\{\mathrm{a, b}\}$
     
  2. $\{\mathrm{b, c}\}$
     
  3. $\{\mathrm{a}, \mathrm{b}, \mathrm{c}\}$
     
  4. $\{\mathrm{a, c}\}$
codeBlocks:
1. a = 1
2. b = a + 1
3. c = a + b
4. a = c + b
5. return a
questions.explanation: After 5: $\{\mathrm{a}\}$ is live (given). After 4: To compute $\mathrm{a=c+b}$, we need $\mathrm{c}$ and $\mathrm{b}$. So $\{\mathrm{c}, \mathrm{b}\}$ are live. After 3: To compute $\mathrm{c}=\mathrm{a}+\mathrm{b}$, we need $\mathrm{a}$ and $\mathrm{b}$. However, $\mathrm{b}$ is also needed for the later instruction (line 4). So $\{\mathrm{a}, \mathrm{b}\}$ are live. Immediately after statement 2, we need both $\mathrm{a}$ and $\mathrm{b}$ to satisfy the requirements of statements 3 and 4 . The live set is $\{\mathrm{a}, \mathrm{b}\}$. GO Classes answered Jan 27 GO Classes comment Share Follow 0 reply Please log in or register to add a comment. questions.questionText: Consider the following lexical specification for a scanner: $\mathrm{KEYWORD\_IF: \verb|if|}$ $\mathrm{ID: [a-z][0-9]*}$ $\mathrm{NUM: [0-9]+}$ The scanner follows the Longest Match rule. In case of a tie in length, the token defined first in the specification takes priority. How many tokens will be generated for the input string "$\verb|if20if|$"?
questions.questionHtml:
Consider the following lexical specification for a scanner:

  1. $\mathrm{KEYWORD\_IF: \verb|if|}$
     
  2. $\mathrm{ID: [a-z][0-9]*}$
     
  3. $\mathrm{NUM: [0-9]+}$
     

The scanner follows the Longest Match rule. In case of a tie in length, the token defined first in the specification takes priority. How many tokens will be generated for the input string "$\verb|if20if|$"?
questions.explanation: The scanner starts at $\verb|i|$. It matches $\verb|if|$ (KEYWORD), but it can also match $\verb|if20|$ as an ID (letter followed by alphanumeric). Following the Longest Match rule, $\verb|if20|$ is a longer match than the keyword if . Thus, the first token is an ID ($\verb|if20|$). The remaining string is if . This matches the KEYWORD_IF . Total tokens$: 2$. questions.questionText: Consider the following three-address code sequence used for a loop: i = 0 L1: t1 = i * 4 t2 = base + t1 val = load t2 i = i + 1 if i < 100 goto L1 Which optimization technique would most effectively transform this code to reduce the number of multiplications inside the loop, and what would be the resulting change to line $2$? Constant Folding; $\verb|t1 = 0|$ Dead Code Elimination; Line $2$ is removed entirely. Strength Reduction; $\verb|t1 = t1 + 4|$ (with initialization $\verb|t1 = 0|$ before the loop).  Loop Unrolling; The loop body is copied $100$ times to remove the branch.
questions.questionHtml:
Consider the following three-address code sequence used for a loop:

i = 0
L1: t1 = i * 4
t2 = base + t1
val = load t2
i = i + 1
if i < 100 goto L1

Which optimization technique would most effectively transform this code to reduce the number of multiplications inside the loop, and what would be the resulting change to line $2$?

  1. Constant Folding; $\verb|t1 = 0|$
     
  2. Dead Code Elimination; Line $2$ is removed entirely.
     
  3. Strength Reduction; $\verb|t1 = t1 + 4|$ (with initialization $\verb|t1 = 0|$ before the loop). 
     
  4. Loop Unrolling; The loop body is copied $100$ times to remove the branch.
codeBlocks:
i = 0
L1: t1 = i * 4
t2 = base + t1
val = load t2
i = i + 1
if i < 100 goto L1

options.label: B
options.text: Dead Code Elimination; Line $2$ is removed entirely.

options.label: C
options.text: Strength Reduction; $\verb|t1 = t1 + 4|$ (with initialization $\verb|t1 = 0|$ before the loop).

options.label: D
options.text: Loop Unrolling; The loop body is copied $100$ times to remove the branch.

questions.explanation: Strength Reduction replaces a "heavy" operation like multiplication inside a loop with a "lighter" one like addition. By initializing $\verb|t1|$ to $0$ and adding $4$ in each iteration, the compiler eliminates the costly $\verb|i*4|$ calculation. questions.questionText: An $\mathrm{LR(1)}$ parser is being constructed for a grammar. If a particular state in the corresponding $\mathrm{LR}(1)$ canonical collection contains the item $[A \rightarrow \alpha \cdot, a]$, which of the following statements is ALWAYS true regarding the behavior of the parser in this state? The parser will perform a reduce action on any input symbol that is $\operatorname{FOLLOW}(A)$. The parser will perform a reduce action ONLY if the current lookahead symbol is $a$. There is a shift-reduce conflict if $a$ is also in $\operatorname{FIRST}(\beta)$ for some item $[B \rightarrow \gamma \cdot a \beta, b]$. Otherwise, an S-R conflict doesn't occur. The parser will transition to a new state regardless of the lookahead symbol.
questions.questionHtml:
An $\mathrm{LR(1)}$ parser is being constructed for a grammar. If a particular state in the corresponding $\mathrm{LR}(1)$ canonical collection contains the item $[A \rightarrow \alpha \cdot, a]$, which of the following statements is ALWAYS true regarding the behavior of the parser in this state?

  1. The parser will perform a reduce action on any input symbol that is $\operatorname{FOLLOW}(A)$.
     
  2. The parser will perform a reduce action ONLY if the current lookahead symbol is $a$.
     
  3. There is a shift-reduce conflict if $a$ is also in $\operatorname{FIRST}(\beta)$ for some item $[B \rightarrow \gamma \cdot a \beta, b]$. Otherwise, an S-R conflict doesn't occur.
     
  4. The parser will transition to a new state regardless of the lookahead symbol.

options.label: A
options.text: The parser will perform a reduce action on any input symbol that is $\operatorname{FOLLOW}(A)$.

options.label: B
options.text: The parser will perform a reduce action ONLY if the current lookahead symbol is $a$.

options.label: C
options.text: There is a shift-reduce conflict if $a$ is also in $\operatorname{FIRST}(\beta)$ for some item $[B \rightarrow \gamma \cdot a \beta, b]$. Otherwise, an S-R conflict doesn't occur.

options.label: D
options.text: The parser will transition to a new state regardless of the lookahead symbol.

questions.explanation: In an LR(1) parser, an item of the form $$ [A \rightarrow \alpha \cdot, a] $$ means: The production $\mathrm{A} \rightarrow \alpha$ is complete. The parser should reduce by $\mathbf{A} \rightarrow \alpha$ only when the lookahead symbol is a. Why option C is false: the parser can shift directly on  $\verb|a|$ if and only if the $\mathrm{LR(1)}$ state contains an item with dot before $\verb|a|$, i.e. $$ [B \rightarrow \gamma \cdot a \beta, b] $$ If the same state also contains $$ [A \rightarrow \alpha \cdot, a] $$ then the parser faces a shift-reduce conflict on $\verb|a|$. questions.explanation: A DAG eliminates redundant sub-expressions. The sub-expression ( $b+c$ ) is computed once $($1st node: $+)$. This result is then multiplied by itself $($2nd node$: ×)$. Finally, the result of the multiplication is added to the original $(b+c)$ result $($3rd node$: +)$. questions.questionHtml:
Consider the following C-style code segment:

while (a < b) {
    if (c < d) x = y + z;
    else x = y - z;
}


Assume this code is translated into Three-Address Code (TAC) using the minimum number of labels required to ensure:

  1. The $\verb|while|$ condition is evaluated at the start of every iteration.
     
  2. The $\verb|if-else|$ control flow correctly branches to either the $\verb|if|$ block or the $\verb|else|$ block.
     
  3. Control returns to the $\verb|while|$ condition check after the $\verb|if-else|$ statement finishes.
     
  4. There is a single exit label immediately following the loop.
     

What is the minimum number of labels required to represent this control flow?
codeBlocks:
L1: if a < b goto L2   // Label 1: Loop Header
    goto L4           // Label 4: Loop Exit

L2: if c < d goto L3  // Label 2: If-Condition
    x = y - z         // Fall-through for 'else'
    goto L1

L3: x = y + z         // Label 3: If-True block
    goto L1

L4: ...               // End of Loop
questions.explanation: L1: if a < b goto L2 // Label 1: Loop Header goto L4 // Label 4: Loop Exit L2: if c < d goto L3 // Label 2: If-Condition x = y - z // Fall-through for 'else' goto L1 L3: x = y + z // Label 3: If-True block goto L1 L4: ... // End of Loop $\text { Minimum number of labels required is } 4$ GO Classes answered Jan 20 GO Classes comment Share Follow 0 reply Please log in or register to add a comment. questions.questionText: Consider the following S-attributed SDT scheme used to calculate the value of an expression. The grammar generates simple arithmetic additions and is suitable for an LR parser. \[ \begin{array}{ll} \text{Production} & \text{Semantic Rules} \\ E \rightarrow E_1 + T & E.\text{val} = E_1.\text{val} + T.\text{val} \\ E \rightarrow T & E.\text{val} = T.\text{val} \\ T \rightarrow \mathbf{id} & T.\text{val} = \mathbf{id}.\text{lexval} \end{array} \] If the input string is $3+5+2$, what is the sequence of values stored on the semantic stack for the attribute val immediately after each reduction of the type $E \rightarrow E_1+T$ occurs? $8,10$ $3, 5, 2$ $3, 8, 10$ $5,2$
questions.questionHtml:
Consider the following S-attributed SDT scheme used to calculate the value of an expression. The grammar generates simple arithmetic additions and is suitable for an LR parser.

\[
\begin{array}{ll}
\text{Production} & \text{Semantic Rules} \\
E \rightarrow E_1 + T & E.\text{val} = E_1.\text{val} + T.\text{val} \\
E \rightarrow T & E.\text{val} = T.\text{val} \\
T \rightarrow \mathbf{id} & T.\text{val} = \mathbf{id}.\text{lexval}
\end{array}
\]

If the input string is $3+5+2$, what is the sequence of values stored on the semantic stack for the attribute val immediately after each reduction of the type $E \rightarrow E_1+T$ occurs?

  1. $8,10$
     
  2. $3, 5, 2$
     
  3. $3, 8, 10$
     
  4. $5,2$
questions.explanation: Initial Reductions: id  $(3)$ is reduced to $T$, then $T$ is reduced to $E$. Stack has $E . v a l=3$. id  $(5)$ is reduced to $T$. Stack now has $E(3)$ and $T(5)$. First $E \rightarrow E_1+T$ Reduction: The parser reduces $E(3)+T(5)$ to a new $E$. E.val $=3+5=\mathbf{8}$. Next Steps: id  $(2)$ is reduced to $T$. Stack now has $E$ $(8)$ and $T$ $(2)$. Second $E \rightarrow E_1+T$ Reduction: The parser reduces $E(8)+T(2)$ to the final $E$. E.val $=8+2=\mathbf{1 0}$. The sequence of values produced by the specific reduction $E \rightarrow E_1+T$ is $\mathbf{8 , 1 0}$. questions.questionHtml:
Let $\mathrm{G}$ be a context-free grammar that is unambiguous, left-factored, and does not have any left-recursion.

Which of the following is true for $\mathrm{G}$ ?

  1. $\mathrm{G}$ is $\mathrm{LL}(1)$.
     
  2. $\mathrm{G}$ may not be $\mathrm{LL}(1)$, but it is definitely $\mathrm{LR}(1)$.
     
  3. $\mathrm{G}$ is not $\mathrm{LR}(1)$.
     
  4. None of the above

options.label: B
options.text: $\mathrm{G}$ may not be $\mathrm{LL}(1)$, but it is definitely $\mathrm{LR}(1)$.

questions.explanation: If a grammar is Left Recursive, then it is Not $\mathrm{LL}(1)$. If a grammar is Not Left Factored, then it is Not $\mathrm{LL}(1)$. If a grammar is Ambiguous, then it is Not $\mathrm{LL}(1)$. However, grammars that are unambiguous, not left recursive and are left factored, may or may not be $\mathrm{LL}(1)$. Consider the grammar: $\mathrm{A} \rightarrow \mathrm{aAa} \mid \varepsilon$ This grammar is unambiguous, left-factored, and does not have any left-recursion, but still it is Not $\mathrm{LL}(1)$, also Not $\mathrm{LR}(1)$. Another example: $\mathrm{S} \rightarrow \epsilon\mid\mathrm{aSa}\mid \mathrm{bSb}$ This grammar is unambiguous, left-factored, and does not have any left-recursion, but still it is Not $\mathrm{LL}(1)$, also Not $\mathrm{LR}(1)$. questions.explanation: The terminal at the beginning of $\gamma$ Given an $\operatorname{LR}(1)$ item $[\mathrm{A} \rightarrow \alpha \bullet \gamma, \delta]$ from a production $\mathrm{A} \rightarrow \beta$, the roles of A , $\alpha, \gamma, \delta$ : A is the nonterminal that is potentially the result of a reduction. $\alpha$ is the portion of $\beta$ that the parser has just seen. $\gamma$ is the portion of $\beta$ the parser will need to see before performing the reduction to $\mathrm{A} . \delta$ is a terminal that must be a lookahead for the reduction to be performed. questions.explanation: Detailed Video Explanation with Complete Analysis:    Since the grammar is ambiguous, so precedence is NOT enforced here. So, we cannot say that $*$ has higher precedence than $+$ or vice versa. Hence, option C is false. questions.questionHtml:
We have a scanner (lexical analyzer) which uses regular expressions to scan an input.

When using regular expressions to scan an input, we resolve conflicts by taking the largest possible match at any point. If two longest matches are of the same length then we give preference to token $\mathrm{T1}$ over token $\mathrm{T2}$.

Consider the string: aba aba aba bab baa aba ab (blank spaces used for readability only & are to be ignored) and its tokenization $: abaa, ~ba, ~ababa, ~bba, ~aa, ~ba, ~a, ~b$

Which of the following lexical analyzer specifications will produce this tokenization?

  1. $\mathrm{T1} : (a b){ }^{*} a^{+} \quad \mathrm{T2}: b^{*} a^{*}$
     
  2. $\mathrm{T1} : (a b)^{*} a^{*} \quad \mathrm{T2}: b^{*} a$
     
  3. $\mathrm{T1} : (a b)^{*} a^{+} \quad \mathrm{T2}: b^{*} a$
     
  4. $\mathrm{T1} : (a b)^{+} a^{+} \quad \mathrm{T2}:b^{*} a^{*}$
questions.explanation: None of the options matches. Using option B, C,we can't tokenzie "b". Also, options A, D do not tokenize the input string in the way the question is asking. questions.questionHtml:
Consider the following grammar $G$ with non-terminals $\{S, A, B, C\}$ and terminals $\{a, b, c, d, g\}$ :

$$
\begin{aligned}
& S \rightarrow A B \\
& A \rightarrow a A \mid \epsilon \\
& B \rightarrow b B \mid C \\
& C \rightarrow c C \mid d \mid \epsilon
\end{aligned}
$$


What is the FOLLOW set of the non-terminal $A$ ?

  1. $\{a, b, c, d\}$
     
  2. $\{b, c, d, \$\}$
     
  3. $\{b, c, d\}$
     
  4. $\{B, b, c, d, \$\}$
questions.explanation: $\{b, c, d, \$\}$ Since $S \rightarrow A B$, $\operatorname{FOLLOW}(\mathrm{A})$ contains $\operatorname{FIRST}(\mathrm{B})$. Because $B$ is nullable ( $\mathrm{B} \rightarrow \mathrm{C} \rightarrow \epsilon$ ), $\operatorname{FOLLOW}(\mathrm{A})$ also inherits $\operatorname{FOLLOW}(\mathrm{S})$, which is $\{\$\}$. questions.questionText: $\text { Consider the following C code segment: }$ inline int square(int s) { return s * s; } void process(int n, int a[]) { int x = 10; int y = x; // Copy of x for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) { a[i] = y * i; int val = square(i); // Assume n is always a multiple of 4 // } } Which of the following is/are not true? THERE IS SCOPE FOR COPY PROPAGATION IN THIS CODE THERE IS SCOPE FOR LOOP UNROLLING IN THIS CODE THE CODE EXHIBITS CONSTANT FOLDING AT RUNTIME THERE IS SCOPE FOR DEADCODE ELIMINATION IN THIS CODE
questions.questionHtml:
$\text { Consider the following C code segment: }$

inline int square(int s) { return s * s; }
void process(int n, int a[]) {
    int x = 10;
    int y = x; // Copy of x
    
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++)
    {
        a[i] = y * i;
        int val = square(i);
        
        // Assume n is always a multiple of 4
        //
    }
}

Which of the following is/are not true?

  1. THERE IS SCOPE FOR COPY PROPAGATION IN THIS CODE
     
  2. THERE IS SCOPE FOR LOOP UNROLLING IN THIS CODE
     
  3. THE CODE EXHIBITS CONSTANT FOLDING AT RUNTIME
     
  4. THERE IS SCOPE FOR DEADCODE ELIMINATION IN THIS CODE

options.label: A
options.text: THERE IS SCOPE FOR COPY PROPAGATION IN THIS CODE

options.label: B
options.text: THERE IS SCOPE FOR LOOP UNROLLING IN THIS CODE

options.label: C
options.text: THE CODE EXHIBITS CONSTANT FOLDING AT RUNTIME

options.label: D
options.text: THERE IS SCOPE FOR DEADCODE ELIMINATION IN THIS CODE

questions.explanation: COPY PROPAGATION (Option A is TRUE): The variable $y$ is assigned the value of $x$. The compiler can replace the use of $y$ in $y * i$ with the constant $10$ , propagating the value and potentially eliminating the variable $y$ entirely. LOOP UNROLLING (Option B is TRUE): Since the loop logic is simple and we are given that $n$ is a multiple of $4$, the compiler can duplicate the loop body and increment $i$ by $4$ each time to reduce the overhead of the condition check ( $i<n$ ). DEAD CODE ELIMINATION (Option D is TRUE): The if $(1==0)$ condition is mathematically impossible to satisfy. The compiler identifies this block as unreachable and can remove it from the final binary to save space. Why Option C is FALSE: As mentioned before, Constant Folding (like changing $5 * 2$ to $10$ ) is a compile-time process. The compiler performs the calculation while building the program so that the CPU doesn't have to do it during execution. Stating it happens at "runtime" is technically incorrect

for (int i = 0; i < n; i++)
{

    for (int j = 0; j < n; j++)

        }

Which one of the following is FALSE?

  1. THE CODE CONTAINS LOOP INVARIANT COMPUTATION
     
  2. THERE IS SCOPE FOR STRENGTH REDUCTION IN THIS CODE

  4. THERE IS SCOPE FOR COMMON SUB-EXPRESSION ELIMINATION IN THIS CODE

options.label: B

options.text: THERE IS SCOPE FOR DEAD CODE ELIMINATION IN THIS CODE

questions.explanation: Loop Invariant Computation (Option A is TRUE): The expression $\verb|int constant_val = a * b + 5;|$ inside the outer loop does not depend on the loop variable $\verb|i|$. It can be moved outside the entire loop structure. Strength Reduction (Option B is TRUE): The expression $\verb|temp = i * 8|$ involves a multiplication. A compiler can replace this with a bitwise shift $(i \ll 3)$ or by using addition in each iteration of the loop, which are "cheaper" operations. Dead Code Elimination (Option C is TRUE): The block $\verb|if (0)| ~\{ ~\ldots ~\}$ will never execute because the condition is always false. The compiler can remove this entire block of code during the optimization phase. Common Sub-expression Elimination (Option D is FALSE): In this specific snippet, there are no identical expressions calculated multiple times that could be replaced by a single variable. questions.questionText: A lexical analyzer uses the following patterns to recognize three tokens $T_1, T_2$, and $T_3$ over the alphabet $\{x, y, z\}$. $$ \begin{aligned} & T_1: x ?(y \mid z)^* y \\ & T_2: y ?(x \mid z)^* x \\ & T_3: z^{+}(x \mid y) ? \end{aligned} $$ $y?$ means $0$ or $1$ occurrence of $y$. The analyzer outputs the token that matches the longest possible prefix. If there is a tie in length, it prioritizes the token with the lowest index $($e.g., $T_1$ over $T_2)$. If the string $zxxyzyx$ is processed by the analyzer, which one of the following is the sequence of tokens it outputs? $T3,~T2,~T1$ $T2, ~T1, ~T2$ $T2, ~T1, ~T3$ $T1,~T2,~T3$
questions.questionHtml:
A lexical analyzer uses the following patterns to recognize three tokens $T_1, T_2$, and $T_3$ over the alphabet $\{x, y, z\}$.

$$
\begin{aligned}
& T_1: x ?(y \mid z)^* y \\
& T_2: y ?(x \mid z)^* x \\
& T_3: z^{+}(x \mid y) ?
\end{aligned}
$$

$y?$ means $0$ or $1$ occurrence of $y$.

The analyzer outputs the token that matches the longest possible prefix. If there is a tie in length, it prioritizes the token with the lowest index $($e.g., $T_1$ over $T_2)$.

If the string $zxxyzyx$ is processed by the analyzer, which one of the following is the sequence of tokens it outputs?
 

  1. $T3,~T2,~T1$
     
  2. $T2, ~T1, ~T2$
     
  3. $T2, ~T1, ~T3$
     
  4. $T1,~T2,~T3$
questions.explanation: Using longext prefix rule, $zxx$ is matches with $T2, ~yzy$ matches with $T1$ and $x$ with $T2$ hence $B$ is correct

$$
\begin{aligned}
& S^{\prime} \rightarrow S \\

& S \rightarrow b \\
& A \rightarrow a A \uparrow \\
& A \rightarrow \epsilon

questions.explanation: We start with the augmented production and expand the closure. $S^{\prime} \rightarrow \bullet S~($Initial$)$ $S \rightarrow \bullet A+S ~($From $S)$ $S \rightarrow \bullet b~($From $S)$ $A \rightarrow \bullet a A \uparrow~($From $A)$ $A \rightarrow \bullet~($From $A$ - this is the $\epsilon$ production$)$ The set $\operatorname{GOTO}\left(I_0, a\right)$ contains the following items: $A \rightarrow a \bullet A \uparrow$ $A \rightarrow \bullet a A \uparrow$ $A \rightarrow \bullet$ The number of items in the set is $\mathbf{3}$. questions.explanation: 1. Evaluating Associativity (Rules for $E$ and $T$ ): For $E \rightarrow E \uparrow T \mid T$ : This is a left-recursive production ($E$ appears as the first symbol on the right side). Evaluating LL(1) Status: A grammar is not LL(1) if it contains left recursion.   • $C \rightarrow a \mid \epsilon$

What is $\operatorname{FIRST}(S)$?

questions.explanation: Option C JAY_THAKAR answered Jan 9 JAY_THAKAR comment Share Follow 0 reply Please log in or register to add a comment. 0 0 votes Answer option C First(S) ={first(AB),first(gh)} First(AB)={first(A)} First(A)={first(CD)} First(CD)={first(C)} First(C)= {a,€} Since C is nullable in CD, we go to the next non terminal symbol i.e., D. Now first(D)= {f}. Since D is also nullable in CD we go to the next non-terminal in AB i.e, B. Now first(B)={b}. (Nullable means having epsilon in its production) Lastly, first(gh)={g}. Finally, First(S) ={a,b,f,g}. Now, the first(S) also contains epsilon even if it does not have epsilon in its production because S is deriving epsilon in one or more steps.( Reference. ) I.e, S=>AB => CD B => €€€=> €. So we can conclude that S can have epsilon in its first set because it can derive the epsilon indirectly. Finally the first set of S is {a,f,b,g,€}. questions.explanation: Item  $\textbf(1):E \rightarrow T$. $+E$ indicates that if the parser sees the symbol $+$ , it can perform a SHIFT action. Item  $\textbf(2):F \rightarrow T$. is a complete item (the dot is at the end), which indicates the parser can perform a REDUCE action. Since the set contains both a Shift possibility on symbol $+$ and a Reduce possibility, it results in a Shift-Reduce conflict. There is only one reduction item $(F \rightarrow T.)$, so there is no Reduce-Reduce conflict. questions.questionText: Consider the following grammar: $E \rightarrow T R$ $R \rightarrow+T R$ $R \rightarrow \epsilon$ $T \rightarrow F Y$ $Y \rightarrow * F Y$ $Y \rightarrow \epsilon$ $F \rightarrow(E)$ $F \rightarrow i d$ What is the FOLLOW(T) for this grammar? $\{+, ), \$\}$ $\{*, +, ), \$\}$ $\{+, \$\}$ $\{*, )\}$
questions.questionHtml:
Consider the following grammar:

  • $E \rightarrow T R$
  • $R \rightarrow+T R$
  • $R \rightarrow \epsilon$
  • $T \rightarrow F Y$
  • $Y \rightarrow * F Y$
  • $Y \rightarrow \epsilon$
  • $F \rightarrow(E)$
  • $F \rightarrow i d$

What is the FOLLOW(T) for this grammar?

  1. $\{+, ), \$\}$
     
  2. $\{*, +, ), \$\}$
     
  3. $\{+, \$\}$
     
  4. $\{*, )\}$
questions.explanation: From $E \rightarrow T R$ : $\operatorname{FOLLOW}(T)$ contains (FIRST(R) - $\{\epsilon\}$ ). $\operatorname{FIRST}(R)$ is $\{+, \epsilon\}$. Therefore, + is added to FOLLOW(T). Handling the $\epsilon$ in $R$ : Since $R \rightarrow \epsilon, \operatorname{FOLLOW}(T)$ must also include everything in FOLLOW( E). Determining FOLLOW $(E)$ : $E$ is the start symbol, so $\$$ is added to FOLLOW( $E$ ). From $F \rightarrow(E)$, the terminal ) follows $E$, so it is added to $\operatorname{FOLLOW}(E)$. Thus, $\operatorname{FOLLOW}(E)=\{\$,)$$\} .$ Combining results: $\operatorname{FOLLOW}(T)=\{+,), \$\}$. questions.questionText: Consider the following snippet of C code int main() { /* Line 1 */     int a = 5, b = 10; /* Line 2 */     if (a < b) then { /* Line 3 */         a = a + 1; /* Line 4 */     } } Identify the compiler's primary response during the compilation process: NO COMPILATION ERROR A LEXICAL ERROR A SYNTACTIC ERROR A SEMANTIC ERROR
questions.questionHtml:
Consider the following snippet of C code

int main() { /* Line 1 */
    int a = 5, b = 10; /* Line 2 */
    if (a < b) then { /* Line 3 */
        a = a + 1; /* Line 4 */
    }
}


Identify the compiler's primary response during the compilation process:

  1. NO COMPILATION ERROR
     
  2. A LEXICAL ERROR
     
  3. A SYNTACTIC ERROR
     
  4. A SEMANTIC ERROR
questions.explanation: LEXICAL ANALYSIS: The scanner looks at the word $\verb|then|$. In many languages (like Pascal or Basic), $\verb|then|$ is a valid keyword. In C, the scanner simply sees the characters $\verb|t-h-e-n|$ and identifies them as a valid identifier (like a variable name). Since it is a valid sequence of characters, there is no Lexical Error. Syntax ANALYSIS : $\verb|if(a < b) then }|$ is not a valid syntax Either $\verb|{ }|$ should come immediately after if or there should be semicolon after then Hence it will generate syntactic error Correct option: C

codeBlocks:
int main() { /* Line 1 */
    int x = 10, y = 5; /* Line 2 */
    int result; /* Line 3 */

}
questions.explanation: LEXICAL ANALYSIS: The scanner sees $\verb|reslt|$ and identifies it as a valid identifier (a string of characters starting with a letter). It does not care if the variable was declared yet. Therefore, there is no lexical error. SYNTACTIC ANALYSIS: The parser checks the structure. It sees $\verb|identifier = identifier + identifier;|$ . This follows the correct grammar for an assignment statement in C. Therefore, there is no syntax error. SEMANTIC ANALYSIS: This is where the compiler checks the Symbol Table . It looks for the declaration of $\verb|reslt|$. Since only $\verb|result|$ (spelled differently) was declared, the compiler realizes $\verb|reslt|$ is an "undeclared identifier." This is a Semantic Error. Correct Answer: D. A SEMANTIC ERROR

Therefore, $\operatorname{FIRST}(R)=\{+, \epsilon\}$. B is TRUE: According to the rule for FOLLOW sets, in a production $A \rightarrow \alpha B$, everything in $\operatorname{FOLLOW}(A)$ is added to $\operatorname{FOLLOW}(B)$. Here, in $E \rightarrow T R, R$ is at the end of the production, so $\operatorname{FOLLOW}(R)=\operatorname{FOLLOW}(E)$. C is FALSE: The symbol $\epsilon$ (epsilon) is never a member of any $FOLLOW$ set. $FOLLOW$ sets only contain terminals and the end-marker $\$$. While $T$ can be followed by things that derive $\epsilon$, the $\epsilon$ symbol itself is not included. D is TRUE: By definition, the end-of-input marker (\$) is always added to the $FOLLOW$ set of the start symbol (in this case, $E$ ). If $X \rightarrow \alpha$ is a production, then everything in $\operatorname{FIRST}(\alpha)$ is added to $\operatorname{FIRST}(X)$. questions.questionHtml:
Which of the following statement(s) is/are FALSE while computing $\textbf{FIRST}$ and $\textbf{FOLLOW}$ sets for a Context-Free Grammar?

  1. If $X \rightarrow \alpha$ is a production, then everything in $\operatorname{FIRST}(\alpha)$ is added to $\operatorname{FIRST}(X)$.
     
  2. The epsilon symbol ( $\epsilon$ ) can be a member of a $\text{FOLLOW}$ set if a non-terminal can derive the empty string.
     
  3. If there is a production $A \rightarrow \alpha B \beta$, then everything in $\operatorname{FIRST}(\beta)$ except $\epsilon$ is added to $\text{FOLLOW(B)}$.
     
  4. For the start symbol $S$, the end-of-input marker $(\$)$ is always placed in $\text{FOLLOW(S)}$.

options.label: A
options.text: If $X \rightarrow \alpha$ is a production, then everything in $\operatorname{FIRST}(\alpha)$ is added to $\operatorname{FIRST}(X)$.

options.label: B
options.text: The epsilon symbol ( $\epsilon$ ) can be a member of a $\text{FOLLOW}$ set if a non-terminal can derive the empty string.

options.label: C
options.text: If there is a production $A \rightarrow \alpha B \beta$, then everything in $\operatorname{FIRST}(\beta)$ except $\epsilon$ is added to $\text{FOLLOW(B)}$.

options.label: D
options.text: For the start symbol $S$, the end-of-input marker $(\$)$ is always placed in $\text{FOLLOW(S)}$.

questions.explanation: A is TRUE: This is the basic rule for computing FIRST sets. If a non-terminal $X$ derives a string $\alpha$, the first terminals of $\alpha$ are also the first terminals of $X$. B is FALSE: The epsilon symbol ( $\epsilon$ ) is never included in a $FOLLOW$ set.$ FOLLOW$ sets only contain terminals and the end-of-input marker (\$). If a non-terminal can derive $\epsilon$, it affects how we calculate the FOLLOW sets of adjacent symbols, but $\epsilon$ itself does not enter the set. C is TRUE: In a production like $A \rightarrow \alpha B \beta$, the symbols that can follow $B$ are exactly the symbols that can start $\beta$. We exclude $\epsilon$ because $FOLLOW$ sets only contain actual lookahead tokens. D is TRUE: By convention, the $FOLLOW$ set of the start symbol always contains the end-marker (\$), signifying the end of the input string. questions.questionHtml:
Which one of the following is FALSE?

  1. A flow graph is a directed graph where nodes represent basic blocks and edges represent the flow of control.
     
  2. Copy Propagation is an optimization that replaces the use of a variable with its assigned value if that value is another variable.
     
  3. Constant Folding can only be performed on local variables within a single basic block and never across a whole function.
     
  4. Dead Code Elimination uses Live Variable analysis to remove instructions that compute values never subsequently used.

options.label: A
options.text: A flow graph is a directed graph where nodes represent basic blocks and edges represent the flow of control.

options.label: B
options.text: Copy Propagation is an optimization that replaces the use of a variable with its assigned value if that value is another variable.

options.label: C
options.text: Constant Folding can only be performed on local variables within a single basic block and never across a whole function.

options.label: D
options.text: Dead Code Elimination uses Live Variable analysis to remove instructions that compute values never subsequently used.

questions.explanation: A is TRUE: This is the standard definition of a Control Flow Graph (CFG). It maps the paths that can be taken during execution. B is TRUE: Copy Propagation replaces instances of a variable (e.g., $x=y$ ) by substituting $y$ for $x$ later in the code to reduce the number of variables and assignments. C is FALSE: Constant Folding (and Constant Propagation) can be performed both locally (within a block) and globally (across the entire function/procedure) using data flow analysis. It is not restricted to a single basic block. D is TRUE: If Live Variable analysis shows that a variable is "dead" (not used before its next assignment), the instruction that assigned its previous value is useless and can be safely deleted via Dead Code Elimination. questions.explanation: A is TRUE: Reaching Definitions is a forward analysis because it tracks which definitions "reach" a point from the preceding code. B is TRUE: Live Variable analysis is backward analysis and is the primary tool used for efficient Register Allocation. C is TRUE: Moving code to a pre-header ensures it runs only once instead of every time the loop iterates. D is FALSE: This is actually Strength Reduction (replacing a heavy operation with a lighter one). questions.questionHtml:
Consider the following ANSI C code segment:
 

w = 5 - y->f_one - x - 2;
for (j = 1; j < 150; j = j + 3)
{
    if (j < w)
    {
        a = a + y->f_two;
        b = b + 5 - x;
    }
    else
    {
        a = a + 5-x;
        b = b + y->f_two;
    }
}


Assumptions:

  1. 1. The variable $\mathbf{y}$ points to a $\verb|struct|$ (allocated on the heap) containing two fields, $\mathbf{f\_one}$ and $\mathbf{f\_two}$.
     
  2. The local variables $\mathbf{w}, \mathbf{x}, \mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b}$, and $\mathbf{j}$ are allotted to registers.
     
  3. Common Sub-expression Elimination (CSE) optimization is applied to the code.
     
  4. Subtraction is treated as an arithmetic operation equivalent to addition for counting purposes (i.e., $A-B$ counts as one operation).

The number of arithmetic operations (addition or subtraction) and the dereference operations (of the form $y \rightarrow f \_one$ or $y \rightarrow f \_two$ ) in the optimized code, respectively, are:
 

  1. $153$ and $2$
     
  2. $149$ and $2$
     
  3. $151$ and $302$
     
  4. $248$ and $152$
questions.explanation: Let's introduce register temporaries $T_1=y \rightarrow f\_one$, $T_2=y \rightarrow f\_two$, and $T_3=5-x$. The temporaries are computed once: $T_1=y \rightarrow f\_one: \mathbf{1}$ dereference. $T_2=y \rightarrow f\_two: \mathbf{1}$ dereference. $T_3=5-x : 1$  arithmetic operation (subtraction). $$ \begin{aligned} & W=5-x-2-T 1 \\\\ & W=T 3-2-T 1 \end{aligned} $$ \[ \begin{array}{lll} \text{Phase} & \text{Arithmetic Operations} & \text{Dereference Operations} \\ \textbf{Initialization} & 1\ \text{(for }T_3\text{)} + 2\ \text{(for }w\text{)} = 3 & 1\ \text{(for }T_1\text{)} + 1\ \text{(for }T_2\text{)} = 2 \end{array} \] The loop runs for $50$ times and in each iteration, no of arithmetic operations performed is $3$ Total no of arithmetic operations performed $=50 * 3+3=153$ Total no of dereference operations performed $= 2$ GO Classes answered Dec 23, 2025 GO Classes comment Share Follow 0 reply Please log in or register to add a comment. 0

codeBlocks:

questions.explanation: Analyzing Line 4: $\verb|result = value @ 5;|$ When the compiler's lexical analyzer (scanner) reaches the character $\verb|@|$ in Line $4$, it attempts to group it with adjacent characters to form a valid C token: It checks if $\verb|@|$ is a valid single-character operator. It is not. It checks if it is part of a multi-character operator (like $\verb|==|$, $\verb|!=|$, etc.). It is not. Since the character $\verb|@|$ is not a valid character for forming any legal token in C (it is not part of an identifier, keyword, constant, or recognized operator), the scanner cannot classify it. This failure to recognize and generate a legal token occurs during the lexical analysis phase and is classified as a lexical error. questions.questionText: A lexical analyzer uses the following regular expressions (REs) to recognize four tokens, $T_1, T_2$, $T_3$, and $T_4$, over the alphabet $\Sigma=\{a, b, c\}$. $T_1:(a \mid b)^* a$ $T_2:(a \mid b)^* b$ $T_3: c(a|b| c)^*$ $T_4:(a|b| c) c$ The analyzer follows two standard rules: Longest Possible Prefix Match: The longest matching prefix is selected. Precedence: If two or more tokens match the same longest prefix, the token rule specified earliest takes precedence ( $T_1>T_2>T_3>T_4$ ). If the analyzer is processing the input string: $$\textbf{bbacabc}$$ What is the complete sequence of tokens generated by the lexical analyzer? $T_2, T_1, T_3$ $T_1,T_3,T_4$ $T_1,T_3$ $T_1,T_3,T_4$
questions.questionHtml:
A lexical analyzer uses the following regular expressions (REs) to recognize four tokens, $T_1, T_2$, $T_3$, and $T_4$, over the alphabet $\Sigma=\{a, b, c\}$.

  • $T_1:(a \mid b)^* a$
     
  • $T_2:(a \mid b)^* b$
     
  • $T_3: c(a|b| c)^*$
     
  • $T_4:(a|b| c) c$
     

The analyzer follows two standard rules:

  1. Longest Possible Prefix Match: The longest matching prefix is selected.
     
  2. Precedence: If two or more tokens match the same longest prefix, the token rule specified earliest takes precedence ( $T_1>T_2>T_3>T_4$ ).
     

If the analyzer is processing the input string:
$$\textbf{bbacabc}$$
What is the complete sequence of tokens generated by the lexical analyzer?

  1. $T_2, T_1, T_3$
     
  2. $T_1,T_3,T_4$
     
  3. $T_1,T_3$
     
  4. $T_1,T_3,T_4$
questions.explanation: Longest prefix "$\text{bba}$" is matched with $T_1,$ Now starting with $\text{c}$, we have only one token  $\rightarrow ~T_3$ which eats the remaining expression. Hence $T_1,T_3$ will be the match here. Option C is correct.

A Syntax-Directed Translation (SDT) scheme is defined for the grammar using synthesized attribute val (value). All operators are assumed to be left-to-right associative for this SDT scheme, regardless of the grammar's structure, and their precedence is determined by the grammar's hierarchy. The rules for evaluation are: 1. Precedence: $\odot$ (Highest) $>\ominus$ (Middle) $>\oplus$ (Lowest). 2. Associativity: All operators evaluate from left-to-right (Left Associative). \[ \begin{array}{ll} \text{Production Rule} & \text{Semantic Rule (Action)} \\[6pt] P \rightarrow Q \oplus P_1 & P.\mathrm{val} = Q.\mathrm{val} + P_1.\mathrm{val} \\[4pt] P \rightarrow Q & P.\mathrm{val} = Q.\mathrm{val} \\[4pt] Q \rightarrow Q_1 \ominus R & Q.\mathrm{val} = Q_1.\mathrm{val} - R.\mathrm{val} \\[4pt] Q \rightarrow R & Q.\mathrm{val} = R.\mathrm{val} \\[4pt] R \rightarrow \text{value} \odot R_1 & R.\mathrm{val} = \text{value}.\mathrm{val} \times R_1.\mathrm{val} \\[4pt] R \rightarrow \text{value} & R.\mathrm{val} = \text{value}.\mathrm{val} \end{array} \] Assuming the terminal value is an integer, what is the computed value of the expression $10 \ominus 5 \oplus 3 \odot 2 ?$
questions.questionHtml:
Consider the following expression grammar with three operators: ⊕, $\ominus$, and $\odot$. A Syntax-Directed Translation (SDT) scheme is defined for the grammar using synthesized attribute val (value). All operators are assumed to be left-to-right associative for this SDT scheme, regardless of the grammar's structure, and their precedence is determined by the grammar's hierarchy.

The rules for evaluation are:

1. Precedence: $\odot$ (Highest) $>\ominus$ (Middle) $>\oplus$ (Lowest).

2. Associativity: All operators evaluate from left-to-right (Left Associative).

\[
\begin{array}{ll}
\text{Production Rule} & \text{Semantic Rule (Action)} \\[6pt]
P \rightarrow Q \oplus P_1 & P.\mathrm{val} = Q.\mathrm{val} + P_1.\mathrm{val} \\[4pt]
P \rightarrow Q & P.\mathrm{val} = Q.\mathrm{val} \\[4pt]
Q \rightarrow Q_1 \ominus R & Q.\mathrm{val} = Q_1.\mathrm{val} - R.\mathrm{val} \\[4pt]
Q \rightarrow R & Q.\mathrm{val} = R.\mathrm{val} \\[4pt]
R \rightarrow \text{value} \odot R_1 & R.\mathrm{val} = \text{value}.\mathrm{val} \times R_1.\mathrm{val} \\[4pt]
R \rightarrow \text{value} & R.\mathrm{val} = \text{value}.\mathrm{val}
\end{array}
\]

Assuming the terminal value is an integer, what is the computed value of the expression $10 \ominus 5 \oplus 3 \odot 2 ?$
questions.explanation: The expression must be grouped based on precedence: © (Highest) → θ (Middle) → ⊕ (Lowest). $$ 10 \ominus 5 \oplus(3 \odot 2) $$ Evaluation within Precedence Groups (Left Associativity) The groups are: Group: $3 \odot 2$. Calculation: $3 \times 2=6$. Remaining Expression: $10 \ominus 5 \oplus 6$. Now, we evaluate the remaining operators $(\ominus, \oplus)$ from left to right as per the problem statement's rule. Step 1 (Leftmost): $10 \ominus$ 5. Calculation: $10-5=5$. Step 2 (Remaining): $5 \oplus 6$. Calculation: $5+6=11$. Consider the grammar defined by the following production rules, with three operators: ⊕ (circle plus), $\ominus$ (circle minus), and $\odot$ (dot operator). The terminal value represents a numerical value.

  • $P \rightarrow Q \oplus P \mid Q$
     
  • $Q \rightarrow Q \ominus R \mid R$
     
  • $R \rightarrow$ value $\odot R \mid$ value

Which one of the following statements about the operators $\oplus, \ominus$, and $\odot$ is TRUE?

  1. The $\ominus$ operator has the lowest precedence (is evaluated last). 
     
  2. The $\oplus$ operator is left associative. 
     
  3. The precedence order is $\odot>\ominus>\oplus$. 
     
  4. The $\odot$ operator is left associative.

options.label: A
options.text: The $\ominus$ operator has the lowest precedence (is evaluated last).

questions.explanation: Operator $\odot$ (Governed by $R$ ): $R$ is built directly from the terminal (value). It is at the base of the expression hierarchy, meaning it must be evaluated first. HIGHEST Precedence. Operator $\ominus$ (Governed by $Q$ ): $Q$ is built from $R$. It is evaluated second. MIDDLE Precedence. Operator $\oplus$ (Governed by $P$ ): $P$ is built from $Q$. It is evaluated last. LOWEST Precedence. Precedence Order: $\odot>\ominus>\oplus$. Associativity Analysis (Determined by Recursion) Operator $\oplus$ (Governed by $P$ ): $P \rightarrow Q \oplus \mathbf{P}$. Right recursion. ⊕ is RIGHT ASSOCIATIVE. Operator $\ominus$ (Governed by $Q$ ): $Q \rightarrow \mathbf{Q} \ominus R$. Left recursion. $\ominus$ is LEFT ASSOCIATIVE. questions.questionText: Consider a language that defines valid identifiers and valid integers. The tokens are defined by the following regular expressions: 1. IDENTIFIER (ID): Must start with a lowercase letter, followed by zero or more lowercase letters or digits. $$ R E_{\mathrm{ID}}=(a|b| \ldots \mid z)(a|b| \ldots|z| 0|1| \ldots \mid 9)^* $$ 2. INTEGER (INT): A non-empty string of digits. $$ R E_{\mathrm{INT}}=(0|1| \ldots \mid 9)^{+} $$ The alphabet $\Sigma$ consists of the $26$ lowercase letters and the $10$ digits ( $\Sigma= \{a, b, \ldots, z, 0,1, \ldots, 9\})$. The minimum number of states in the Deterministic Finite Automaton (DFA) that recognizes the combined language $L=L(\mathrm{ID}) \cup L(\mathrm{INT})$ is $\_\_\_\_$
questions.questionHtml:
Consider a language that defines valid identifiers and valid integers. The tokens are defined by the following regular expressions:


1. IDENTIFIER (ID): Must start with a lowercase letter, followed by zero or more lowercase letters or digits.

$$
R E_{\mathrm{ID}}=(a|b| \ldots \mid z)(a|b| \ldots|z| 0|1| \ldots \mid 9)^*
$$


2. INTEGER (INT): A non-empty string of digits.

$$
R E_{\mathrm{INT}}=(0|1| \ldots \mid 9)^{+}
$$


The alphabet $\Sigma$ consists of the $26$ lowercase letters and the $10$ digits ( $\Sigma= \{a, b, \ldots, z, 0,1, \ldots, 9\})$.

The minimum number of states in the Deterministic Finite Automaton (DFA) that recognizes the combined language $L=L(\mathrm{ID}) \cup L(\mathrm{INT})$ is $\_\_\_\_$
questions.explanation: 1. Initial States: We need an initial state  $(S_0)$ which represents the start of scanning. 2. Recognizing INT: From $S_0$, on any digit $(0-9)$, move to state $S_1$. $S_1$ is an accepting state for INT. From $S_1$, on any digit, stay in $S_1$. 3. Recognizing ID: From $S_0$, on any letter $(a-z)$, move to state $S_2$. $S_2$ is an accepting state for ID. From $S_2$, on any letter or digit, stay in $S_2$. 4. Handling Conflicts/Errors: From $S_0$, on an error input (e.g., non-digit, non-letter like $\verb|#|$), move to a Trap/Error state  $(S_E)$. From $S_1$, on any letter (which is not allowed for INT), move to the Trap state $(S_E)$. From $S_2$, on any other input (like $\verb|#|$), move to $S_E$. Minimum no of states $=4$ GO Classes answered Dec 11, 2025 GO Classes comment Share Follow See 1 comment 1 1 comment reply Aman Shukla commented Apr 4 reply Follow flag answer shuld be 3 @Suresh Babu 1 0 0 reply Share Please log in or register to add a comment. 0 0 votes 4 JAY_THAK

f = 3 * a + 3 * b;


When generating the overall compiler intermediate representation for optimization, these blocks are represented internally.

Assuming the constant folding optimization $3 \times(a+b)$ is applied, the minimum number of nodes in the Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) for the entire set of expressions $\textbf{c, d, e, f}$ that are computed after the preceding block $\mathbf{B0}$ is $\_\_\_\_$
questions.explanation: Optimization Step (Line $f$ ) : Apply constant folding/strength reduction: $\verb|f = 3 * a + 3 * b;| \rightarrow \verb|f = 3 * (a + b);|$ GCSE Analysis (Input from $B 0$ ): $\textbf{B0}$ computes $a+b$, and stores the result in $\mathbf{x}$. The value $a+b$ is available. Computing $c, d, e, f$ (Minimal DAG Nodes): $\mathbf{c}=\mathbf{a}+\mathbf{b}$ ; This value is already computed in $B 0$ and stored as $\mathbf{x}$. No new node needed. REUSE $\mathbf{x}$'s value. $\mathbf{d}=\mathbf{x*2}$ ; Requires $x$ (from $B 0$ ) and the constant $\mathbf{2}$. $\mathbf{e}=\mathbf{2*x}$ ; This is the same operation as $x * 2$ (due to commutativity). REUSE the node for $d$. $\mathbf{f}=(\mathbf{3*(a+b)})$ ; This is equivalent to $3 * x$. Requires the constant $\mathbf{3}$ and the value $\mathbf{x}$. Leaf Nodes (Inputs/Constants needed after $B0$): The value of $\mathbf{x}$ (the result of $a+b$ ). The constant $\mathbf{2}$ . The constant $\mathbf{3}$ . Total: $\mathbf{3}$ LEAF NODES Interior Nodes

questions.explanation: Dependency $L_3 \rightarrow L_5$ (The potential WAR): $L_3$ : Reads $\mathbf{A}[\mathbf{i}]$ (The location at index $i$) $L_5$ : Writes $\mathbf{A}[\mathbf{k}]$ (The location at index $k$) Since $L_4$ sets $\mathbf{k}=\mathbf{i}$, the locations are guaranteed to be the same: $\mathbf{A}[\mathbf{i}]$ is the same memory cell as $\mathbf{A}[\mathbf{k}]$. $L_3$ reads $\mathbf{A}[\mathbf{i}]$. $L_5$ writes $\mathbf{A}[\mathbf{i}]$. questions.questionText: Consider the following two sets of $\mathrm{LR}(1)$ items of an $\mathrm{LR}(1)$ grammar. \[ \begin{array}{l|l} \text{Set } I_1 & \text{Set } I_2 \\ \hline S \rightarrow A \cdot b,\ \mathbf{c} / d & S \rightarrow A \cdot b,\ \mathbf{a} / \mathbf{s} \\ A \rightarrow \cdot e,\ \mathbf{b} & A \rightarrow \cdot e,\ \mathbf{b} \\ A \rightarrow \cdot f,\ \mathbf{b} & A \rightarrow \cdot f,\ \mathbf{b} \end{array} \] Which of the following statements related to merging of the two sets in the corresponding LALR parser is/are FALSE ? Cannot be merged since the kernel items have different look-ahead sets. Can be merged and will not result in any Shift-Reduce (S-R) or Reduce-Reduce (R-R) conflicts. Can be merged but will result in a Reduce-Reduce (R-R) conflict on look-ahead symbol b. Cannot be merged because the GOTO action on symbol $\mathbf{b}$ from $I_1$ and $I_2$ would lead to different target LR(1) states.
questions.questionHtml:
Consider the following two sets of $\mathrm{LR}(1)$ items of an $\mathrm{LR}(1)$ grammar.

\[
\begin{array}{l|l}
\text{Set } I_1 & \text{Set } I_2 \\
\hline
S \rightarrow A \cdot b,\ \mathbf{c} / d & S \rightarrow A \cdot b,\ \mathbf{a} / \mathbf{s} \\
A \rightarrow \cdot e,\ \mathbf{b} & A \rightarrow \cdot e,\ \mathbf{b} \\
A \rightarrow \cdot f,\ \mathbf{b} & A \rightarrow \cdot f,\ \mathbf{b}
\end{array}
\]


Which of the following statements related to merging of the two sets in the corresponding LALR parser is/are FALSE?

  1. Cannot be merged since the kernel items have different look-ahead sets.
     
  2. Can be merged and will not result in any Shift-Reduce (S-R) or Reduce-Reduce (R-R) conflicts.
     
  3. Can be merged but will result in a Reduce-Reduce (R-R) conflict on look-ahead symbol b.
     
  4. Cannot be merged because the GOTO action on symbol $\mathbf{b}$ from $I_1$ and $I_2$ would lead to different target LR(1) states.

options.label: A
options.text: Cannot be merged since the kernel items have different look-ahead sets.

options.label: B
options.text: Can be merged and will not result in any Shift-Reduce (S-R) or Reduce-Reduce (R-R) conflicts.

options.label: C
options.text: Can be merged but will result in a Reduce-Reduce (R-R) conflict on look-ahead symbol b.

options.label: D
options.text: Cannot be merged because the GOTO action on symbol $\mathbf{b}$ from $I_1$ and $I_2$ would lead to different target LR(1) states.

questions.explanation: Two LR(1) sets can be merged into a single LALR(1) set if and only if they have the same kernel items. Kernel of $I_1:\{S \rightarrow A \cdot b, ~A \rightarrow \cdot e, ~A \rightarrow \cdot f\}$ Kernel of $I_2:\{S \rightarrow A \cdot b, ~A \rightarrow \cdot e, ~A \rightarrow \cdot f\}$ Since the kernel items are identical (disregarding the look-aheads), the two sets CAN be merged. The merged LALR(1) set $I_{12}$ contains no Reduce items, therefore, it cannot have an S-R or R-R conflict. Statement 4: Cannot be merged because the $\textbf{GOTO}$ action on symbol $\mathbf{b}$ from $I_1$ and $I_2$ would lead to two different sets. FALSE. Since $I_1$ and $I_2$ have identical kernels, $\operatorname{GOTO}\left(I_1, b\right)$ and $\operatorname{GOTO}\left(I_2, b\right)$ will lead to two $\operatorname{LR}(1)$ sets that are mergeable (i.e., they have the same kernel). The GOTO actions do not prevent the merging of $I_1$ and $I_2$. Hence $1,3,4$ are false GO Classes answered Dec 6, 2025 G

questions.questionHtml:
Consider the following code segment:

\[
\begin{array}{l}
\verb|z = a - b;|\\
\verb|x = 3 * z;|\\
\verb|y = z + 10;|\\
\verb|z = x + y;|\\
\verb|a = y / 2;|\\
\verb|x = a * z;|
\end{array}
\]
The minimum number of total variables required to convert the above code segment to static single assignment form is $\_\_\_\_$ .
questions.explanation: \[ \begin{array}{ccc} \text{Line} & \text{Original Variable} & \text{New SSA Version Created} \\ (1) & z & z_{1} \\ (2) & x & x_{1} \\ (3) & y & y_{1} \\ (4) & z & z_{2} \\ (5) & a & a_{1} \\ (6) & x & x_{2} \\ \end{array} \] We count the unique variable versions required: 1. Definitions in Code: $\mathbf{z_1}, \mathbf{x_1}, \mathbf{y_1}, \mathbf{z_2}, \mathbf{a_1}, \mathbf{x_2}$ ($6$ unique versions) 2. Used Inputs (Original Versions): $\mathbf{a}$ (used in line $1$) and $\mathbf{b}$ (used in line $1$). ($2$ unique versions) $$ \begin{gathered} \text { Total SSA Variables }=(\text { New Versions Created })+(\text { Input Variables Used }) \\\\ \qquad \text { Total SSA Variables }=6+2=\mathbf{8} \end{gathered} $$ The minimum number of total variables required is $\mathbf{8 .}$ GO Classes answered Dec 4, 2025 GO Classes comment Share Follow 0 reply Please log in or register to add a comment. 1 1 vote In SSA - In the entire program

questions.explanation: A variable is considered "live" at a point in the program if its current value might be used later on some execution path before being redefined. This statement uses the value of  i  (on the right side) but defines  k  (on the left side). questions.questionText: Given the following expression grammar: $$ \begin{gathered} E \rightarrow E+T|T * E| T \\ T \rightarrow T / F \mid F \\ F \rightarrow \mathrm{id} \end{gathered} $$ Which of the following is/are true? $*$ has higher precedence than $+$ $/$ has higher precedence than $*$ $+$ is left-associative $*$ is right-associative
questions.questionHtml:
Given the following expression grammar:

$$
\begin{gathered}
E \rightarrow E+T|T * E| T \\
T \rightarrow T / F \mid F \\
F \rightarrow \mathrm{id}
\end{gathered}
$$


Which of the following is/are true?

  1. $*$ has higher precedence than $+$
     
  2. $/$ has higher precedence than $*$
     
  3. $+$ is left-associative
     
  4. $*$ is right-associative
questions.explanation: Given grammar: $E \rightarrow E \,+\, T \;\mid\; T \,*\, E \;\mid\; T$ $T \rightarrow T \,/\, F \;\mid\; F$ $F \rightarrow id$ ---------------------------- ● Operator appearance by grammar level: The operator $/$  appears in the rule for $T$:     $T \rightarrow T \,/\, F$ The operators $+$ and $*$ appear in the rules for $E$:     $E \rightarrow E \,+\, T \;\mid\; T \,*\, E$ Since $T$ is lower in the grammar hierarchy than $E$, any parsing involving $/$ must complete before any reductions that involve $+$ or $*$.   Thus $/$ binds more tightly than both $+$ and $*$ (i.e., it has higher precedence). ---------------------------- ● Associativity $+$ is left-associative because $E \rightarrow E \,+\, T$ is left-recursive $*$ is right-associative because $E \rightarrow T \,*\, E$ is right-recursive $/$ is left-associative because $T \rightarrow T \,/\, F$ is left-recursive ---------------------------- ● Final Evaluation of statements: A. * has higher preced

questions.questionText: The minimum number of arithmetic operations required to evaluate the polynomial $$ P(X)=2 X^6-3 X^5+4 X^4-X^3+5 X^2+6 X-7 $$ for a given value of $X$, using only one temporary variable, is:
questions.questionHtml:
The minimum number of arithmetic operations required to evaluate the polynomial

$$
P(X)=2 X^6-3 X^5+4 X^4-X^3+5 X^2+6 X-7
$$

for a given value of $X$, using only one temporary variable, is:
questions.explanation: $$ P(X)=2 X^6-3 X^5+4 X^4-X^3+5 X^2+6 X-7 $$ Factor $X$ from first 6 terms: $$ P(X)=X\left(2 X^5-3 X^4+4 X^3-X^2+5 X+6\right)-7 $$ Again: $2 X^5-3 X^4+4 X^3-X^2+5 X+6=X\left(2 X^4-3 X^3+4 X^2-X+5\right)+6$ So: $$ P(X)=X\left(X\left(2 X^4-3 X^3+4 X^2-X+5\right)+6\right)-7 $$ Again: $2 X^4-3 X^3+4 X^2-X+5=X\left(2 X^3-3 X^2+4 X-1\right)+5$ So: $$ P(X)=X\left(X\left(X\left(2 X^3-3 X^2+4 X-1\right)+5\right)+6\right)-7 $$ Again: $2 X^3-3 X^2+4 X-1=X\left(2 X^2-3 X+4\right)-1$ So: $$ P(X)=X\left(X\left(X\left(X\left(2 X^2-3 X+4\right)-1\right)+5\right)+6\right)-7 $$ Again: $2 X^2-3 X+4=X(2 X-3)+4$ So: $$ P(X)=X(X(X(X(X(2 X-3)+4)-1)+5)+6)-7 $$ 1. $t \leftarrow 2 \cdot X$ (1 mult) 2. $t \leftarrow t-3$ (1 add) 3. $t \leftarrow t \cdot X+4$ (1 mult + 1 add) 4. $t \leftarrow t \cdot X-1$ (1 mult + 1 add) 5. $t \leftarrow t \cdot X+5$ (1 mult + 1 add) 6. $t \leftarrow t \cdot X+6$ (1 mult + 1 add) 7. $t \leftarrow t \cdot X-7$ (1 mult + 1 add) Total $=6+6=12$ operations. questions.excerpt: The minimum number of arithmetic operations (additions and multiplications) required to evaluate the polynomial$$P(X)=X^5+3 X^4+2 X^3+7 X^2+8 X+9$$for a given value of $X...
questions.questionText: The minimum number of arithmetic operations (additions and multiplications) required to evaluate the polynomial $$ P(X)=X^5+3 X^4+2 X^3+7 X^2+8 X+9 $$ for a given value of $X$, using only one temporary variable, is:
questions.questionHtml:
The minimum number of arithmetic operations (additions and multiplications) required to evaluate the polynomial

$$
P(X)=X^5+3 X^4+2 X^3+7 X^2+8 X+9
$$

for a given value of $X$, using only one temporary variable, is:
questions.explanation: $$ P(X)=X^5+3 X^4+2 X^3+7 X^2+8 X+9 $$ Factor $X$ from first 5 terms: $$ P(X)=X\left(X^4+3 X^3+2 X^2+7 X+8\right)+9 $$ Again: $X^4+3 X^3+2 X^2+7 X+8=X\left(X^3+3 X^2+2 X+7\right)+8$ So: $$ P(X)=X\left(X\left(X^3+3 X^2+2 X+7\right)+8\right)+9 $$ Again: $X^3+3 X^2+2 X+7=X\left(X^2+3 X+2\right)+7$ So: $$ P(X)=X(X(X(X(X+3)+2)+7)+8)+9 $$ Let $t=X$ $t \leftarrow X+3$ $t \leftarrow t \cdot X+2$ $t \leftarrow t \cdot X+7$ $t \leftarrow t \cdot X+8$ $t \leftarrow t \cdot X+9$ That's $4$ multiplications and $5$ additions $\rightarrow$ $9$ operations. questions.questionHtml:
Arrange the following parsers in increasing order of their power of handling grammars i.e. from the least powerful parser to the most powerful parser.

  1. $\mathrm{LR}(0)$
  2. $\mathrm{LR}(1)$
  3. $\mathrm{LALR}(1)$
  4. $\mathrm{LL}(0)$
  5. $\mathrm{SLR}$

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

  1. $\mathrm{LL}(0) \rightarrow \mathrm{LR}(0) \rightarrow \mathrm{SLR} \rightarrow \mathrm{LR}(1) \rightarrow \mathrm{LALR}(1)$
  2. $\mathrm{SLR} \rightarrow \mathrm{L R}(0) \rightarrow \mathrm{L L}(0) \rightarrow \mathrm{L R}(1) \rightarrow \mathrm{L A L R}(1)$
  3. $\mathrm{LL}(0) \rightarrow \mathrm{LR}(0) \rightarrow \mathrm{SLR} \rightarrow \mathrm{LALR}(1) \rightarrow \mathrm{LR}(1)$
  4. $\mathrm{LR}(0) \rightarrow \mathrm{LL}(0) \rightarrow \mathrm{SLR} \rightarrow \mathrm{LR}(1) \rightarrow \mathrm{LALR}(1)$

options.label: B
options.text: $\mathrm{SLR} \rightarrow \mathrm{L R}(0) \rightarrow \mathrm{L L}(0) \rightarrow \mathrm{L R}(1) \rightarrow \mathrm{L A L R}(1)$

questions.explanation: The correct order of parsers from least powerful to most powerful in handling grammars is LL(0) → LR(0) → SLR → LALR(1) → LR(1) . This sequence reflects their increasing complexity and ability to handle a wider range of context-free grammars. D. LL(0) : This is a predictive parser that makes decisions based on the current input symbol and the top of the stack. It's the least powerful as it can only handle a very restrictive set of grammars. The "(0)" indicates that it has no lookahead. A. LR(0) : This is a bottom-up parser that can handle a larger class of grammars than LL(0). It constructs a parse tree from the leaves up to the root, but it also has no lookahead, which can lead to shift/reduce or reduce/reduce conflicts. E. SLR : This is an extension of LR(0) that uses one symbol of lookahead to resolve some of the conflicts that LR(0) cannot handle. The 'S' stands for Simple .
